(p-454)

Surah "Al-Hashr" (The Gathering)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ It is reported that this surah was revealed in its entirety concerning the Banu al-Nadir. That is because "when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, the Banu al-Nadir made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that they would neither be against him nor with him. But when he prevailed on the day of Badr, they said: 'This is the Prophet whose description is in the Torah.' Then, when the Muslims were defeated on the day of Uhud, they doubted and broke the treaty. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf went out with forty riders to Makkah, and he formed an alliance with Abu Sufyan at the Ka'bah. So the Prophet ﷺ ordered Muhammad ibn Maslamah al-Ansari, and he killed Ka'b by treachery. Then the Prophet ﷺ went out with the army against them, and he besieged them for twenty-one nights, and he ordered that their palm trees be cut down. When Allah cast terror into their hearts, they sought peace, but he refused to accept from them anything except exile, on condition that each three of them could carry on one camel whatever goods they wished from their belongings. So they departed to Syria, to Ariha and Adhri'at."

﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book﴾, meaning the Jews of Banu al-Nadir,

﴿from their homes﴾, in Medina. The lam in ﴿at the first gathering﴾ is connected to "expelled." It is the same lam as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Oh, would that I had sent forth [good deeds] for my life﴾ [al-Fajr: 24], and in the saying "I came to him for such-and-such a time." That is, He expelled those who disbelieved at the first gathering. The meaning of "the first gathering" is that this was their first gathering to Syria. They were from a tribe that had never before been expelled, and they were the first of the People of the Book to be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula to Syria. Alternatively, this was their first gathering, and their last gathering was the expulsion carried out by Umar from Khaybar to Syria. Their last gathering is the gathering of the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Whoever doubts that the place of gathering is in Syria, let him recite this verse. They are the first gathering, and the rest of mankind is the second gathering." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said to them when they departed: "Go forth, for you are the first gathering, and we are following in your footsteps." Qatada said: "When the end of time comes, a fire will come from the direction of the east and gather people to the land of Syria, and there the Resurrection will take place over them." It has also been said that the meaning is: He expelled them from their homes at the first time they were gathered for fighting, because it was the first fight the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fought against them.

﴿You did not think that they would go forth﴾, because of the severity of their might, their strength, the firmness of their fortresses, and the abundance of their numbers and equipment.

﴿And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah﴾. That is, they thought their fortresses would protect them from the might of Allah. The difference between this construction and the structure in which it came is that placing the predicate before the subject indicates their excessive confidence in the fortresses' strength and their protection of them. Making their pronoun the subject indicates that the sentence is attributed to them, showing their belief about themselves that they were in honor and protection, so that they paid no attention to anyone who might confront them or hope to attack them. This is not the case in your saying: "And they thought that their fortresses would protect them."

﴿But Allah came at them﴾, that is, the command of Allah and His punishment. In the irregular readings (shawadh, variant readings not in the standard transmission) it is read "fa-ātāhumu Allāhu," meaning Allah brought them destruction.

﴿from where they did not expect﴾, from where they did not suppose or imagine, and it had not occurred to them. This was the killing of their chief, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, by surprise, at the hand of his foster brother.

﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾, that is, fear.

﴿They destroyed their houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers﴾. "Yukhribūna" is read by Abu 'Amr. "Al-takhrīb" and "al-ikhrāb" mean causing corruption by tearing down and demolishing, and "al-kharbah" means ruin. They used to destroy their interiors while the Muslims destroyed their exteriors, because of what Allah willed of uprooting their affairs and that no house of theirs should remain in Medina and no one of them should remain there. What led them to destroy was their need for the wood and stones, so that they could block the mouths of the alleys with them, and so that they would not regret, after their expulsion, that these buildings remained as dwellings for the Muslims, and so that they could carry with them the fine wood and teak that was in their buildings. As for the believers, what prompted them to destroy was to remove their stronghold and to widen the field of battle for them. The meaning of their destroying it with the hands of the believers is that, when they exposed them to the breaking of the covenant for that purpose and were the cause of it, it was as if they had commanded them to do it and charged them with it.

﴿So take warning, O you with insight﴾. That is, reflect on what befell these people and on the cause that made them deserve it. Beware of doing the same as they did, lest you be punished with the same punishment as theirs. This is evidence for the permissibility of qiyas (analogical reasoning).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 3:

﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them the exile﴾, i.e., the going out from the homeland, together with (their) family and children,

﴿He would have punished them in this world﴾, by killing and taking captives, as He did with the Banu Qurayza,

﴿and for them﴾, whether they were exiled or killed,

﴿in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire﴾, which has nothing more severe than it.
That is because they opposed God, defying Him, and His Messenger, [and whoever opposes God and His Messenger] (the opposition being to Him and to His Messenger). Indeed God is severe in punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 5:

﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down⁠—﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of "whatever you cut down." The position (mahall) of "ma" is in the accusative, governed by "qata'tum" (you cut down), as if it were said: "What did you cut down?"

The pronoun referring back to "ma" in His words ﴿or you left them standing on their roots﴾ is feminine, because it carries the sense of "al-linah" (the palm tree). "Al-linah" is of the category "al-alwan" (the colours or varieties), and its ya' (y) is substituted for a waw (w); it was changed because of the kasra before it. It is also said that "al-linah" means the noble palm tree, as though they derived it from "al-lin" (softness, tenderness).

﴿standing upon their roots, then by Allah's permission﴾: cutting them down and leaving them were both by Allah's permission.

﴿and that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾: that He might humiliate the Jews and enrage them. He permitted their cutting down.

(p-457) ﴿And what Allah granted as fay' (spoils gained without battle) to His Messenger﴾, He made it exclusively his,

﴿from them﴾, from the Banu al-Nadir, ﴿you did not make any expedition against it with horses or camels﴾. That was not by the galloping of horses or camels from you against it. And "al-rikab" (الرِّكابُ) means camels. The meaning is: you did not spur horses or camels in obtaining and seizing it, nor did you exert yourselves in fighting for it. Rather, you walked to it on your feet, because it was two miles from Madinah, while the Prophet ﷺ was on a donkey, and that was all.

﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills﴾. That is, what Allah bestowed upon His Messenger of the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir was not something you obtained through fighting and overpowering, but Allah gave him power over them and over what was in their hands, just as He gave His messengers power over their enemies. So the matter concerning it is left to him, to place it wherever he wills, and he does not divide it in the manner of the spoils of war that were fought for and taken by force and compulsion. He distributed it among the Muhajirun (the Emigrants), and he gave none of the Ansar (the Helpers) except three of them, because of their poverty.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 7:

﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near kinsfolk and the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer﴾. And the reason the conjunction (al-'atif) did not enter upon this sentence is that it is an explanation (bayan) of the first, so it is part of it, not foreign to it. It explained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) what he should do with what Allah restored to him, and commanded him to place it where the one-fifth (khums) of the spoils is placed, divided among the five categories. Some of the exegetes rejected this view and said: The first verse was revealed concerning the property of the Banu al-Nadir, and Allah made it exclusively for His Messenger, whereas this verse concerns the spoils of every town that is taken by the strength of the raiders. And in the verse is an explanation of the disposition of its one-fifth, so it is a new beginning (mubtada'a).

﴿So that it does not become a circulating commodity﴾: "takūna dawlatun" ("becomes a circulating commodity"), with "yazīdu" (increases), upon "kāna" (the complete/full verb). "Al-dawlah" and "al-dawlah" are that which circulates for a person, meaning it turns over from fortune (al-jidd). The meaning of His saying ﴿so that it does not become a circulating commodity among the rich among you﴾ is: so that the restored property, whose right is to be given to the poor so that it may be their sustenance by which they live, does not become a fortune circulating among the rich, multiplying by it.

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you﴾, i.e., whatever he gives you of the division of spoils or restored property,

﴿take it﴾, accept it,

﴿and whatever he forbids you from﴾, from taking it,

﴿refrain﴾ from it, and do not seek it,

﴿and fear Allah﴾, lest you oppose him and neglect his commands and prohibitions,

﴿indeed Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever opposes the Messenger of Allah (p-458) (ﷺ). The more correct view is that it is general to everything the Messenger (ﷺ) gave and forbade, and the matter of the restored property falls within its generality.

﴿For the poor﴾ is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for His saying ﴿and to the near of kin﴾, and for the word it is conjoined to (*ma'tuf 'alayhi*). What prevented making it a substitute for ﴿for Allah and for the Messenger﴾, although the meaning is for the Messenger of Allah, is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, removed His Messenger from the poor in His saying ﴿and they help Allah and His Messenger﴾, and because He exalts the Messenger of Allah above being called "poor." Also, making it a substitute according to the apparent wording would contradict what is required in glorifying Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿the emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties﴾ refers to those in Mecca. This is evidence that the unbelievers come to own the properties of the Muslims by seizure, because Allah (Exalted) called the emigrants "poor," even though they had homes and properties.

﴿seeking﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

﴿grace from Allah and approval﴾ means they seek Paradise and the approval of Allah.

﴿and they help Allah and His Messenger﴾ means they help the religion of Allah and assist His Messenger.

﴿those are the truthful﴾ means in their faith and their striving.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 59, verse 9:

﴿And those who﴾ is in the genitive (*ma'tuf*) on "*al-Muhajirin*" (the Emigrants, ال مهاجرين), and they are the Helpers (*al-Ansar*).

﴿settled in the abode﴾ means they settled in Madinah.

﴿and the faith﴾ means they made their faith sincere (*akhlasu al-iman*), like his saying:

*"I fed her chaff and cold water..."* (poetry, incomplete in the source)

Or: they made faith a settled and established place for them, because of their firmness and steadfastness upon it, just as they made Madinah such a place. Or he meant the abode of emigration (*dar al-Hijrah*). He placed the definite article (*lam al-ta'rif*) in "*al-dar*" in place of the genitive complement, deleted the first term of "*dar al-iman*" (the abode of faith), and put the second term (*al-mudaf ilayhi*) in its place.

﴿before them﴾ means before the Emigrants, because they preceded them in settling in the abode of emigration and of faith. It was also said: before their emigration.

﴿they love those who emigrate to them﴾ to the extent that they shared their wealth with them and lodged them in their own homes. It is related that a man who had two wives gave up one of them, so that a man from the Emigrants could marry her.

﴿and they find in their breasts no need for what they have been given﴾ means they do not feel in themselves any craving for something they need from what the Emigrants were given of the *fay'* (spoils returned to the Muslims without battle) and other things. The "needed thing" is called "*hajah*" (need). The meaning is that their souls did not pursue what was given to others, and did not aspire to anything of it that they needed. It was also said: "*hajah*" means envy of what was given to the Emigrants from the *fay'*, since the Prophet ﷺ gave it specially to them. It was also said: the reading means "they find in their breasts no need from the loss of what they have been given," so both genitive complements have been deleted.

﴿and they prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in need﴾ — *khasasah* means poverty. Its root is "*khisas al-bayt*," which refers to the gaps of a house. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*), meaning: their poverty being assumed. It is related that a man among them hosted a guest; he put the children to sleep, served the food, and extinguished the lamp, so that he would feed his guest while he himself did not eat. It is related from Anas: "A roasted sheep's head was given as a gift to one of them, and he was in need, so he sent it to his neighbour, and nine souls passed it around until it returned to the first." Abu Zayd said: "A young man from the people of Balkh said to me: What is asceticism (*al-zuhd*) among you? I said: When we find, we eat; and when we lose, we are patient. He said: This is how the dogs of Balkh behave among us. Rather, when we lose, we are patient, and when we find, we prefer others."

﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾, meaning those who attain what they wanted. "*Shuhh*" (stinginess) is baseness, and it means that a man's soul is tight-fisted and greedy in withholding. As for *bukhl* (miserliness), it is withholding itself. It was also said: "*shuhh*" is consuming your brother's property unjustly, and "*bukhl*" is withholding your own property. It is related from Kisra: "Stinginess is more harmful than poverty, because the poor man expands when he finds (something), unlike the stingy man."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 10:

﴿And those who came after them﴾: this is also coordinated (ʿatf) with "the Emigrants" (al-Muhajirin). They are those who emigrated afterwards. It is also said: they are the Followers (al-tabiʿun) who follow them in goodness. It is also said: it refers to those after them until the Day of Resurrection. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Everyone who is born in Islam until the Day of Resurrection has entered into this fay'." So the waw is for coordination in both cases. And it is also read: "li-alladhina" (for those who) in both places.

﴿They say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any ghill (rancour) toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate and Merciful.﴾ It is said: they are the Emigrants and the Helpers (al-Ansar). ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "They were commanded to seek forgiveness for them, but they reviled them."

Ghill: hiqd (resentment, spite).

﴿Toward those who believe﴾: meaning the Companions (al-Sahaba).

﴿Our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate and Merciful﴾. It was said to Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib: "What do you say about ʿUthman, Talha and al-Zubayr?" He said: "I say what Allah has said to me," and he recited this verse.

Then He marvelled at His Prophet with His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 11:

﴿Have you not seen those who played the hypocrite﴾, i.e., have you not seen, O Muhammad, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his partisans,

﴿who say to their brothers who disbelieved from among the People of the Book﴾, meaning the Banu al-Nadir, and what is meant is the brotherhood of disbelief,

﴿If you are expelled﴾, from your homes,

﴿we will surely go out with you﴾. It is related that Ibn Ubayy and his companions secretly sent word to the Banu al-Nadir when the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged them: "Do not come out of the fortress. If they fight you, we are with you; we will not abandon you. And if you are expelled, we will surely go out with you."

﴿And we will not obey anyone concerning you﴾, in your fighting,

﴿ever, ever﴾, from the Messenger of Allah and the Muslims, even if they force us to it, or in abandoning you and breaking the promise of support we made to you.

﴿And if you are fought, we will surely help you; but Allah testifies that they are liars﴾, in their promises to the Jews. In this there is evidence for the truth of prophethood, because it is a report of the unseen.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 12:

﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them; and if they are fought, they will not help them; and if they help them, they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be helped.﴾

And He said, "and if they help them," after informing that they will not help them, on the basis of supposition and hypothesis, like His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. And just as He knows what will happen, He knows what will not happen, were it to happen, how it would happen. The meaning is: "And if the hypocrites help the Jews, the hypocrites will be defeated, then they will not be helped after that," i.e., Allah will destroy them, and their hypocrisy will not benefit them, because their disbelief has become manifest. Or: the Jews will be defeated, then the help of the hypocrites will not benefit them.

(p-461) ﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome﴾ — meaning: more feared. It is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of "ruhiba," the passive form. His words ﴿in their breasts﴾ indicate their hypocrisy (nifāq): that is, they show you the fear of Allah openly, while in their hearts you are more awe-inspiring to them ﴿than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾ — that is, they do not know Allah and His greatness, such that they would fear Him as He truly deserves to be feared.

﴿They will not fight you﴾ means they will not be able to fight you,

﴿all together﴾, gathered together, referring to the Jews and the hypocrites,

﴿except﴾ being,

﴿in fortified towns﴾, protected by trenches and walls,

﴿or from behind walls﴾. The word "جِدارٍ" (jidar, "wall," singular) is read as "جُدُرٍ" (judur, plural). Makki and Abu 'Amr read it as "جِدارٍ" (jidar).

﴿Their might among themselves is fierce﴾. This means that the fierce might for which they are described exists only among themselves, when they fight one another. If they were to fight you, that might and strength would not remain for them, because the brave man becomes a coward when confronting the war of Allah and His Messenger.

﴿You think them﴾, that is, the Jews and the hypocrites,

﴿to be all together﴾, gathered, possessing unity and solidarity,

﴿while their hearts are divided﴾, scattered, with no unity between them. This means that there is enmity and hostility among them, so they do not truly support one another. This is an encouragement to the believers and a strengthening of their hearts for fighting them.

﴿That﴾, the division,

﴿is because they are a people who do not reason﴾. The scattering of hearts weakens their strength and helps (against) their spirits.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 15:

﴿Like those who were before them﴾: that is, their example is like the example of the people of Badr (Badr), so the subject (mubtada') has been omitted.

﴿shortly before﴾: that is, they settled in the period shortly before them.

﴿They tasted the evil consequence of their affair﴾: the bad outcome of their disbelief and their enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It comes from their saying: "kala' wabil," meaning: unwholesome, of bad outcome. That is, they tasted the punishment of killing in this world.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾: that is, in addition to that, in the Hereafter they will have the punishment of the Fire.

﴿Like the example of Satan when he says to man, "Disbelieve." But when he disbelieves, he says, "Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ [p-462] That is: the example of the hypocrites in inciting the Jews to fight, promising them victory, then abandoning them and breaking their word, is like the example of Satan when he leads a man astray by his scheming and then disowns him at the end. It is also said that the reference is to his (Satan's) enticing of the Quraysh on the day of Badr, and his saying to them, ﴿No one can overcome you today from among the people, and indeed I am your protector,﴾ [al-Anfal: 48] up to his saying, ﴿Indeed, I am free of you﴾ [al-Anfal: 48].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 17:

﴿So it was that the end of both of them⁠—﴾ the end of the disbelieving human being and of the Shaytan (Satan),

﴿that they are both in the Fire, abiding therein forever.﴾ "ʿĀqibatahumā" is the predicate (khabar) of "kāna," placed before its subject. "Anna" together with its noun and predicate, that is, "fī al-nār" (in the Fire), is in the position of the nominative, as the subject (ism). "Khālidayn" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾

O you who believe, fear Allah, [by complying] with His commands, so do not oppose them.

﴿And let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow﴾. He used the indefinite "soul" (nafs) to indicate fewness, meaning few are the souls that look at what they have sent ahead for the Hereafter. "Tomorrow" means the Day of Resurrection. He called it by the name of the day that follows your day, to bring it near, or he expressed the Hereafter as "tomorrow," as though this worldly life and the Hereafter were two days: a today and a tomorrow. Its being indefinite (nakirah) is to magnify its matter, meaning that its reality is not known because of its greatness. It is related from Malik ibn Dinar: "Written on the gate of Paradise: (What we did, we found; what we put forward, we profited by; what we left behind, we lost)."

﴿And fear Allah﴾: he repeated the command to be God-conscious (taqwa) for emphasis. Or it means: fear Allah in performing the obligations, since it is joined to what is an action, and fear Allah in abstaining from sins, since it is joined to what serves as a warning, namely: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾. In this is an exhortation to vigilance (muraqabah), for whoever knows at the time of committing an act that Allah is aware of the sins he is committing will refrain from them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 19:

﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah﴾, who abandoned the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and what He commanded them, (p-463) ﴿so He caused them to forget themselves﴾, so He abandoned them from His remembrance with mercy and success,

﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾, those who have gone out of obedience to Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 20:

﴿Not equal are the companions of the Fire and the companions of Paradise. The companions of Paradise—they are the triumphant.﴾ This is an alert for people and a notification that, owing to the extremity of their heedlessness, their scant reflection on the outcome, their eagerness to prefer the immediate (al-'ajilah, this worldly life) and to follow desires, it is as though they do not know the difference between Paradise and the Fire, and the vast gulf between their companions, and that the great triumph is with the companions of Paradise while the painful punishment is with the companions of the Fire. It is therefore their duty to know this and to be alerted to it, just as you say to one who disobeys his father, "He is your father," treating him as one who does not know him, thereby alerting him to the right of fatherhood which requires dutifulness and tenderness. The Shafi'is have used this verse as evidence that a Muslim is not to be killed for killing a disbeliever, and that a disbeliever does not acquire ownership of a Muslim's property by seizure (al-istila'). We have answered the like of this in "Usul al-Fiqh" (the Principles of Jurisprudence) and "al-Kafi" (the Sufficient).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 59, verse 21:

﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart out of fear of Allah﴾. That is: owing to the greatness and majesty of the Qur'an, if discernment were placed in the mountain and the Qur'an were sent down upon it, it would have humbled itself (khasha'a), that is, submitted and bowed down, and it would have split (tasaddaʿa), that is, cracked apart, out of fear of Allah. It is also permissible that this is a figurative expression (tamthil), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust (al-amanah)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. This is supported by His saying: ﴿And these are the parables We present to the people, that perhaps they will reflect﴾, where "these" refers to this parable and to its like in various places of the revelation. The purpose is to rebuke the human being for the hardness of his heart and his scant humility when reciting the Qur'an and reflecting upon its admonitions and its warnings. Then He responded to those who associated partners with Allah and likened Him to His creation, so He said:

He is Allah, other than whom there is no god, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed (ʿālim al-ghayb wa-l-shahāda)(ﷺ not applicable). That is: the secret and the public; or: the world and the Hereafter; or: the non-existent and the existent.

﴿He is the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾

(p-464) ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King﴾, whose kingship never ceases.

﴿The Holy (al-Quddus)﴾, the One exalted above all defects. In the glorification of the angels: "Most Holy, Most Pure, Lord of the angels and the Spirit."

﴿The Source of Peace (al-Salam)﴾, the One from whose injustice creation is safe. From al-Zajjaj.

﴿The Giver of Security (al-Mu'min)﴾, the Bestower of safety. And from al-Zajjaj: the One who grants the creatures security from His injustice. Or: the Granter of security from His punishment to whoever obeys Him.

﴿The Guardian (al-Muhaymin)﴾, the Watcher over everything, the Preserver of it. It is on the pattern of "mufay'il," derived from "al-amn" (security), except that its hamzah has been changed into a haa.

﴿The Almighty (al-'Aziz)﴾, the Victorious, who is never overcome.

﴿The Compeller (al-Jabbar)﴾, the Exalted, the Great, before whom those beneath Him are humbled. Or: the One Great in might and dominion. Or: the Subduer, possessor of irresistible power.

﴿The Majestic (al-Mutakabbir)﴾, the One perfect in greatness and majesty.

﴿Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him﴾: He has exalted His essence above what the polytheists attribute to Him.

He is Allah, the Creator (al-Khaliq), the one who determines what He brings into existence.

Al-Bari' (the Originator), the one who brings into existence.

Al-Musawwir (the Fashioner), in the wombs.

﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾: those which indicate the sublime attributes.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Almighty, the Wise﴾: He concluded the surah with what He began it with.

On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "I asked my beloved, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), about the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam), and he said: 'Take upon yourself the end of Surat al-Hashr, and recite it often.' So I repeated the question, and he repeated the answer to me; I repeated it again, and he repeated it to me again."
